title: Painting at the court
hook: Sikh and hill painters made portraits of the court and the Gurus

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patna and Nanded, and your line was gifts to the guru's places. What small gift did you give? Today, a different kind of gift: pictures. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

Picture a small painting of the kind made for the Lahore court. An old man sits on a cushion in plain clothes, with a white beard, and nothing about him shouts that he's the king. Around him stand courtiers in bright turbans, in reds and golds and greens. No camera ever caught Ranjit Singh. What we have instead is paint, laid on by hand with fine brushes, by artists who worked for his court. Today: painting at the court.
screen: `A SMALL PAINTING.` → `A PLAIN KING AMONG BRIGHT TURBANS.` → `PAINTED FOR THE COURT.`

segments.voice: First, the painters. Some came down from the hill kingdoms north of the Punjab plains, places like Guler and Kangra, with a tradition of small, careful paintings in bright color. As those hill states came under Lahore's power, painters found new patrons at the Sikh court and among its nobles. Sikh artists painted alongside them. Second, what they painted: the court. Portraits of the Maharaja, his sons and his ministers, his generals on horseback, courtiers in a row. Some portraits show the Maharaja himself plainly dressed, among a richly dressed court. Third, what they painted: the Gurus. Painters made portraits of the Gurus, among them Guru Nanak with his companions Bhai Bala and Bhai Mardana, Mardana with his rabab. These images were never photographs. No painter of that time had ever seen the Gurus. The painters were imagining, with devotion, faces they knew only from stories and hymns. Sikhs today hold different views on such pictures. Some hang them in homes with love, some say the Guru is the Word, not a face, and a picture should never become an object of worship. The Sikh code of conduct rejects the worship of images. And fourth, why it matters. These paintings are one way later generations can still see that court: its colors, its clothes, its faces. A kingdom remembered in paint.
screen: `PAINTERS FROM THE HILLS AND THE PUNJAB.` · `PORTRAITS OF THE COURT.` · `THE GURUS IMAGINED WITH DEVOTION.` · `A KINGDOM REMEMBERED IN PAINT.` · then, large: `THE COURT IN PAINT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a painting. If you can, find a Sikh painting, from a book, a museum's website, or a picture on someone's wall, and look at it now. If you can't, call one up in your mind. Take it slowly. Look at the faces first, then the hands, then the colors, then the edges. Notice one detail you'd normally miss: a fold of cloth, a bird, the shape of a turban. Ask what the painter wanted you to see. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Painting at the court. Hill and Sikh painters who made portraits of the Lahore court and imagined the Gurus with devotion. Today's word.
Your line: the court in paint. Today, look slowly at one picture you usually walk past, and find a detail you never noticed. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Sikh paintings from the Lahore court era are kept in museums and collections, and some Sikh homes display later pictures of the Gurus; the Sikh code of conduct rejects the worship of images.
